Team lead's note, written for myself, Thursday.

Damini has been on my team for a year. Three times this month her partner has called during lunch and I've heard him mock her loudly on speaker: her cooking, her job, her friends. Each time she laughs and says, "That's just his way. He doesn't mean it."

Today, after another call, her hands were shaking as she typed. I asked if she had a minute. I said once, gently, "The way he spoke to you didn't sound kind. You deserve respect." She looked away and said, "You don't know him."

I didn't argue. I told her my door is open, any time, and gave her the number for our employee counselling line. She put the card in her bag. I'll keep checking in, quietly.

qa.a: Three times this month.

qa.q: How does the note-writer feel after Damini's shaking hands and her reply?
qa.a: The note-writer feels concerned and uneasy, but chooses patience instead of pushing Damini.

qa.q: Why was naming it once and staying available a wise approach?
qa.a: It lets Damini know someone sees it without forcing her to defend her partner, and the counselling number gives her a safe next step.

qa.q: How might Damini be feeling when she says "You don't know him"?
qa.a: Damini may feel defensive and embarrassed, and perhaps not ready to face how the calls affect her.

grounding: A team lead notices a colleague dismissing a partner's repeated disrespect, names it gently once and stays available.

Saturday night

Went for dinner with Sachin and his boyfriend. The boyfriend corrected everything Sachin said, rolled his eyes at his stories, and called him "useless" twice in front of the waiter. Sachin just smiled.

Later, on the walk to the metro, Sachin said, "He's just blunt. It's how he is."

I wanted to list every moment. I wanted to shout. But I've seen friends dig in harder when you push.

So I said it once. "It bothered me, how he spoke to you. You don't deserve that." Sachin went quiet, then changed the subject.

I didn't bring it up again. But I told him I'm around, any day, any hour.

I hope he knows I meant it. — Samir

qa.a: Samir felt angry and upset, wanting to shout and list every moment, but held back.

Vaibhav, fifteen, had just got his first pair of glasses. Walking into his class in the small town, he was sure every eye was on him. When two girls whispered, he thought they were laughing at his glasses.

At the tuition centre that evening, he snapped at his friend Tanuja. "You're all judging me."

"Judging you for what?" Tanuja asked.

"The glasses. I look stupid."

Tanuja shook her head. "Nobody even said anything. The girls were talking about the cricket match."

Vaibhav was quiet. He had looked at himself in the mirror that morning and thought, stupid. Maybe the stares were his own.

I'm Binita, and last year my flatmate Yash told me I was secretly angry with him. He said, "You're so cold. I know you hate me."

I was shocked. I didn't feel any of that. We'd had a small fight about rent weeks earlier, but I had let it go.

At first I started to believe him. Maybe I was cold? I lay awake, wondering.

Then I made myself look at the facts. I'd cooked for him that week. I'd covered his electricity share when he forgot. I'd said good morning every day.

Next day I said calmly, "Yash, I'm not angry. Are you still upset about the rent?" He looked at the floor. "Maybe I am."

That was when I understood.

qa.q: What had Binita covered when Yash forgot?
qa.a: His electricity share.

qa.q: How did Binita feel when Yash said "I know you hate me"?
qa.a: Binita felt shocked and confused, then started to doubt and lay awake wondering.

qa.q: What did Binita do instead of absorbing the accusation?
qa.a: Binita checked the facts, like cooking for Yash and covering his share, then calmly asked if Yash was still upset.

qa.q: How might Yash have felt when Binita asked about the rent?
qa.a: Yash probably felt caught and a bit ashamed, admitting he was still upset.

grounding: A student accused of secret anger by a flatmate calmly checks the facts, and the grudge turns out to be the flatmate's.

At nineteen, in my first year of college, my roommate kept saying, "Why do you hate me? You're so cold." I didn't hate her. I was just shy and busy.
